question: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening shortness of breath and fatigue. Her paternal uncle had similar symptoms and died of respiratory failure at 45 years of age. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Pulmonary function testing shows an FVC of 84%, an FEV1/FVC ratio of 92%, and a normal diffusion capacity. An ECG shows a QRS axis greater than +90 degrees. Genetic analysis shows an inactivating mutation in the bone morphogenetic protein receptor type II (BMPR2) gene. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "BMPR2 mutation" -> "dysregulated vascular smooth muscle proliferation" -> "pulmonary arterial hypertension" -> "elevated pulmonary arterial pressure" -> "shortness of breath and fatigue" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Family history of respiratory failure" -> "genetic predisposition" -> "BMPR2 mutation" -> "pulmonary vascular remodeling" -> "elevated pulmonary arterial pressure" -> "symptoms of dyspnea and fatigue" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Normal lung auscultation" -> "absence of parenchymal lung disease" -> "normal diffusion capacity" -> "rules out fibrosis" -> "focus on vascular cause" -> "elevated pulmonary arterial pressure" -> 85%
CHAIN: "ECG shows right axis deviation" -> "right ventricular strain" -> "secondary to pulmonary hypertension" -> "elevated pulmonary arterial pressure" -> "symptoms of dyspnea and fatigue" -> 90%
analysis: The patient's symptoms, family history, and genetic findings are indicative of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). The inactivating mutation in the BMPR2 gene is a well-known genetic cause of familial PAH. The normal diffusion capacity and the ECG findings further support the diagnosis of PAH, as they suggest right heart strain without significant parenchymal lung disease or left heart disease. Elevated pulmonary arterial pressure is the most likely cause of her symptoms.
